extracted.intended_audience: CIE IGCSE English Language (Paper 2) students preparing for narrative writing
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for producing a successful narrative response to Section B (Composition) of the Cambridge IGCSE English Language Paper 2, including task constraints, planning, and what examiners reward in content, structure, style and accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Task length and options
rubrics_metrics.description: You will have a choice of two descriptive writing options: Question 4 or 5. You are required to write about 350-450 words, which is approximately 2-3 sides of A4 in standard-sized handwriting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stay within the 350–450 word guideline to meet exam expectations and avoid being penalised for extreme brevity or excessive length. Choose one of the two provided options (Q4 or Q5).

rubrics_metrics.name: Time allocation and planning
rubrics_metrics.description: You will have one hour in which to complete the task. You should spend 15 minutes planning your writing, and 45 minutes writing your response (including 5 minutes at the end to re-read and check your work).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan your route through the composition and how it will end before you start writing. Use planning time to decide structure, key events, perspective and key vocabulary/phrases to achieve effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marks allocation
rubrics_metrics.description: The task is worth 40 marks: up to 16 marks for content and structure, and up to 24 marks for style and accuracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand both strands — content/structure and style/accuracy — and allocate effort accordingly (strong ideas and organisation plus engaging language and correct mechanics).

rubrics_metrics.name: Content and structure (16 marks)
rubrics_metrics.description: The plot is well-defined and strongly developed with features of fiction writing such as description, characterisation, effective climax and convincing details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shape a narrative including moments of tension and drama; plan and deliver a clear plot arc (build-up, climax, resolution). Avoid merely 'telling' a sequence of events — create structure and purposeful ordering. Start at your story’s main setting rather than a long journey/build-up. Consider how characters and events support the story's message and how the ending resolves or reinforces it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style and accuracy (24 marks)
rubrics_metrics.description: The writing contains precise, well-chosen vocabulary and varied sentence structures chosen for effect. Language and tone are suitable for the context. Spelling, punctuation and grammar are almost always accurate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose vocabulary and sentence structures carefully to create specific effects; vary sentence and paragraph lengths to keep style and tone dynamic; avoid over-complicating language—simple words and sentences can be powerful. Ensure high accuracy in spelling, punctuation and grammar to avoid losing marks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality and use of detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Be convincing and original in your use of detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid clichés or over-used narratives (example given: abandoned cabins in the woods). Use fresh, specific details to make scenes and characters believable and memorable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Answering the question and interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure that your response is a well organised and thoughtful interpretation of whichever title you choose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carefully consider the two question choices and plan your route through your composition, including how it will end, before you start writing. Make sure your interpretation addresses the prompt in a way that is coherent and purposeful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterisation
rubrics_metrics.description: Use characterisation to create believable protagonists and characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include characters’ thoughts and feelings, not just what happens, so readers understand motives and reactions. Use characters to represent the 'message' of the story where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative perspective
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the narrative perspective which will work most effectively for your story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose first/third person or other perspectives deliberately to shape tone, intimacy and reliability; be consistent and use perspective to enhance character insight or narrative tension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding over-reliance on dialogue
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only use dialogue if it drives forward the plot and you are able to punctuate it correctly. Dialogue should reveal character, advance action or create tension rather than substitute for narrative description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy of language and atmosphere
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure that all of the words you choose contribute to the overall atmosphere and effect you want to create.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trim irrelevant detail; every sentence/word should build mood, character or advance the plot. Consider the 'message' of your story and how diction and imagery reinforce it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pacing and structural choices
rubrics_metrics.description: Vary your sentence and paragraph lengths to keep the style and tone dynamic; include an effective climax.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use shorter sentences and paragraphs to speed up action or create tension; longer sentences for reflection or description. Structure scenes to build toward a convincing climax and resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language registers and simplicity
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not over-complicate your language unnecessarily.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not underestimate the power of simple words and sentences to create powerful effects. Use clear, appropriate register for the task rather than flashy or irrelevant vocabulary.
